content: Cefixime is indicated for the treatment of acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by susceptible strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. The recommended dosage is 400 mg per day, administered orally as a single daily dose or divided into two doses every 12 hours. It is also used to treat otitis media caused by H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Streptococcus pyogenes, with the same dosage regimen. For pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by S. pyogenes, the same dosage applies, and treatment should continue for at least 10 days. Cefixime serves as an alternative treatment for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhea when ceftriaxone is unavailable. However, it is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment per CDC guidelines. The preferred regimen includes 400 mg of cefixime orally once, combined with 1 g of azithromycin orally once, or alternatively, doxycycline 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days. For uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli and Proteus mirabilis, the dosage is 400 mg per day orally, either as a single dose or divided every 12 hours. In children aged 6 months to 12 years weighing ≤45 kg, the dosage is 8 mg/kg/day orally, either as a single dose or divided every 12 hours. For those over 12 years or weighing >45 kg, the adult dosage of 400 mg/day applies. Safety and efficacy in children under 6 months have not been established. Cefixime is contraindicated with live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG and typhoid vaccines, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. Similarly, coadministration with the cholera vaccine should be avoided, as systemic antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Cefixime may interact with other medications. It can increase the toxicity of aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, tobramycin, streptomycin, and plazomicin) by enhancing nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution and close monitoring are advised when coadministered with these drugs. It may also increase the effects of warfarin, necessitating careful monitoring of coagulation parameters. Probenecid can increase cefixime levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Cefixime may reduce the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab). Caution and monitoring are recommended during coadministration. Additionally, cefixime may alter intestinal flora, potentially reducing the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives and other medications dependent on gut microbiota for activation, such as sodium picosulfate. Adverse effects of cefixime include diarrhea (16%), abdominal pain, candidiasis, dizziness, dyspepsia, elevated liver enzymes, eosinophilia, erythema multiforme, fever, flatulence, headache, increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine, leukopenia, nausea, prolonged prothrombin time, pruritus, pseudomembranous colitis, rash, serum sickness-like reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, thrombocytopenia, urticaria, vaginitis, and vomiting. Hypersensitivity reactions have been documented, and caution is advised in patients with a history of penicillin allergy. Prolonged or repeated use of cefixime may lead to superinfections or overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, including fungi. Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia has been reported, necessitating monitoring of hematologic parameters during and after therapy. Therapy should be discontinued if hemolytic anemia occurs. Cefixime may also cause a fall in prothrombin activity, particularly in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, or those on prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Monitoring of prothrombin time and administration of vitamin K may be required. Severe cutaneous reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), have been reported. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if such reactions occur. Acute renal failure, including tubulointerstitial nephritis, has also been reported. Therapy should be stopped if renal failure occurs, and supportive treatment should be initiated. In pregnant women, available data from observational studies and case reports have not established an association between cefixime use and major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. However, maternal gonorrhea is associated with risks such as preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal transmission, which can lead to neonatal complications. There is no data on cefixime presence in human milk, but it is present in animal milk. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for cefixime and potential adverse effects on the infant. Cefixime is generally well-tolerated but requires dosage adjustments in severe renal insufficiency to avoid central nervous system toxicity, including seizures. It has limited activity against anaerobes and should be used cautiously in patients with a history of gastrointestinal disease. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefixime. If CDAD is suspected, ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile should be discontinued, and appropriate management should be initiated.
